utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth and interpreters, to the legal assistants, registrar, Prosecution and Defence. I see they're all there. Good morning to the accused. Today we're going to take up the testimony that we started yesterday if there are no other matters pending, and I don't think there are. I should like to call upon the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. I should like to remind you that you are continuing your testimony under oath. Do you feel rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to continue answering questions put to you by Ms. Hollis. Ms. Hollis, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Examined by Ms. Hollis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness AT. Yesterday before the adjournment for the day we had begun to discuss things that had occurred in the Omarska camp, and today with the first questions I ask you, I'd like to continue with that line of inquiry. While you were in the Omarska camp, during the day while you were in the kitchen area, did you see detainees being abused while they were brought for their meals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often would you see this occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every shift, every day. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men who came for meals, what was the condition of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dirty, unshaven, unkept, their clothes in tatters, long hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you notice about the smell of these people as they came for meals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a terrible stench when they passed by. And they would always run by us, they didn't go slowly, so you could feel this stink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how strong was this stench?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I felt like vomiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were detained in the Omarska camp, did you know a man by the name of Travancic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the SUP. He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the SUP. I don't know what he did, but later on he opened his own private weapons shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say a private weapons shop, are you talking about a legal shop, a lawful activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A normal shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this man in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him there, would you please describe his condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was all bloody and black and blue, and all -- his clothes all torn. He couldn't walk properly. He had to be led by the people with him, the Muslims. He couldn't even hold his own plate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see your husband while you were held in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He looked completely crazy. He had lost a lot of weight. His neck was very thin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him there, were you ever able to observe any type of injuries or bruising on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any injuries on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a woman by the name of Sadeta Medunjanin before you were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see her in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw her in the camp, what was her condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a completely changed woman. I hardly recognised her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had lost a lot of weight. Her hair had gone grey. It wasn't combed. It was unkept. Her skirt was kept up by a sort of rubber band to stop it from slipping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was she held in the camp while you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the day, did you ever see her give food to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She gave her bread to her son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the night when she was called out from your room and taken from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the night between the 27th and 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after she was called out, what did you and other women from your room do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all cried. We saw her out of the room, and when she went down, some of the women, the women that could, went to the WC to see where she had gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the WC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a bus underneath the window and there was a person there of Serb ethnicity reading out a list, and the detainees who were there would get into the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you looked out the window, did you see Sadeta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see Sadeta very well. Probably she wasn't on the list yet, the list hadn't come to her name, but she left in that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how was it that you were able to look out and see this? How were you able to see these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I saw Sadeta had changed. And I went into the toilet to see if I could see. The window was fairly high up. I stepped up onto the bath and stretched a little to see where they were going, because some of my family was going in that bus too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this bus, do you remember about where it was positioned as you looked out the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was below the window where the police was. The police was upstairs and this was downstairs. So I could look through the window, peek through the window from the other building, from the other side of the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these people that you saw being put on the bus, were these men or women that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were men, and that night those two women were called out as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the other woman who was called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other woman was from the other room. I don't know her name. I can't remember her name. But we talked about her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually hear any of the names that were being called out from this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just Sadeta was on the list. I didn't hear the rest. Just during the day while we were sitting around, we saw the movement of people from the "white house" to the halls, and we assumed that they were the people that were being separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw this movement of people, was this before or after the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw this bus, did you see any sort of writing or anything on this bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it said "Seselj." That's what I was able to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the Omarska camp, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by whom were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man I didn't know. Later on, I learnt that he was from Prijedor, from Tukovi. He was tall and fair and wore a camouflage uniform. There was another man with him who worked in the SUP in Prijedor whom I knew, and he was wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this interrogation take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upstairs, on the floor above, where the kitchen is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this interrogation, what, if anything, were you able to hear from the hallway and from the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cries of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were held in the Omarska camp, did you ever see any of the detainees receiving any medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever receive any medical treatment while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were detained in Omarska, did you ever see bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every evening when they took them with the yellow truck. One day I saw them being thrown out of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the day you saw these bodies being thrown out of the "white house," what was done with these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were ordered, that is to say, the detainees who were there, they were ordered to throw water over them and that if there was any movement among those bodies, that those who moved were to be taken back to the "white house." The other ones were to be taken away. They took them by a fence, and I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These bodies that you saw taken away in a truck, where were these bodies laying before they were taken away in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fence, the hedge. They were all put there on a heap. The fence was a little further off from the kitchen but you could still see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the Witness could please be shown Exhibit 3/82.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, if you could take a moment to look at this photograph and orient yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could give it first to the witness, please. Now, if this could please be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These bodies laying by this hedge or fence, could you show us where that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hedge was here and the bodies were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are pointing to an area on the photograph that is near to a small red building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that red building is parallel with the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you would see a truck come to pick up those bodies. How were you able to see this truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here. It was 7.00, and we women were going into the rooms where we slept. There were curtains across the whole window. There was a point here, like a checkpoint. There was a covered table and three or four men of Serb ethnicity there, and they allegedly guarded us. The truck went this way, and we could see through the curtains -- we could see the truck through the curtains. We could see arms and legs, the bodies of men hanging out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the truck, the route that the truck would take would be from the "red house" on the restaurant side, the kitchen side of the building, past the kitchen area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you pointed to an area where there was some type of checkpoint or guard place, and that place was -- as we look at the photograph, would be below the "white house" on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is where it was, facing the kitchen. Facing our premises, that's where it was. There was a table there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be removed, please. And if we could please now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session, Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, were you ever taken from your sleeping room at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Omarska, that is 23 days, I was taken out several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who took you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladjo Krkan did. Mladjo Radic, nicknamed Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in general terms, could you tell the Court what happened on these times that he took you from your sleeping room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took me out to make himself coffee or tea, to watch TV, to have a glass of beer. Each time he took me out, he would have a different pretext for that. Once he brought me a small gift from an association of women, and once, on one occasion when he took me out, he had his way with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean he had his way with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took me to a room, which I didn't like right away, and I was sexually assaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These times that he took you out to make coffee or tea for him or to watch television or to have a glass of beer, to what room did he take you to do these things?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the room you earlier called the commanders' room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would he take you out to have a glass of beer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he also drinking beer on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He gave me a glass of beer, but I refused. I made some coffee, and I refused to watch TV. Then I made some tea, and I accepted that small gift which had been sent to me by a former colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you were sexually assaulted, in what room did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room was located at the end of the corridor on the left-hand side. It was a huge room with a writing desk inside, and there was a sponge mattress on the floor in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3/77B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, I would ask you to take a moment to look at this diagram, and then if you could please put that on the overhead, and if you could show the Judges what room it was you were taken to when you were sexually assaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what that room was used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it used to be a conference room that meetings -- where meetings were held. It had a very large oval table in it. And later on when we were there, it was used for women to be taken in because no one needed a sponge mattress for a meeting. That was quite clear to me right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That can be removed, please. And I would ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us go back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask details, that is why I've asked for a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in public session, Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, when most people were transferred from the Omarska camp, how many men remained behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred and seventy-two men, according to my assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 3rd of August, when people were being called out for transfer, were you able to see who was calling them out for transfer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how close were you to him when he was calling these people out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could read the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could read them. How were they written down? What were they on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On white pieces of paper, quite thick; that is to say, there were lots of men and women written in. The women who were to stay, their names were underlined in red pencil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ask Prcac why people's names were underlined in red?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "What has been crossed out in red, those are staying. The others are going somewhere else, to another place."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified earlier about Prcac. Did you see him in the camp during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I went up to him on one occasion in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you address him by any sort of title or rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I went up to him, I said "commander" because I assumed that he was a little higher up than the others. I said, "Will you tell me the truth? (redacted) (redacted)." And he said, "We'll see." And I wanted to know why I was being held there. Was it only because I was a Muslim or because of something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you addressed him as commander, what, if anything, did he say to you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "We'll see." That was what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted), were you taken from the Omarska camp to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you reunited with your family members there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you held in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) I went to Trnopolje, and the 1st of October was when I left. There were 36 buses going to Karlovac, and I was among them, and the whole of my family, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have testified about Krkan and about Prcac. Have you seen either of these men since 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1992? Where? Where do you mean, where did I see them? I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before, but during the camp time, I did. I saw them in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we have a problem with either my language or the translation. Let me try this again. Since 1992, after 1992, have you seen either of these men again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1992. On the 26th of May, the war broke out. When I came to Omarska, that's when I saw them. Later on when I went to Trnopolje I did not see them, nor did I see them before 1992. Just during the period I spent at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the years since 1992, I'm talking about the years 1993 to 2000, to now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- have you ever seen either of these men again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen them on television or in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what media have you seen them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen them on cassettes and different media (redacted). I watch television, and as soon as he appeared, I recognised their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at liberty, when I had left detention and when I got electricity and got a television set, then I saw them. You could see them. It was showing, until I came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what year that was that you saw them, or years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was from 1993, 1994, 1995, I can't remember the years. I saw cassettes and the media, television. I can't give you a date, so I don't want to specify any year. I wouldn't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, do you think you would be able to recognise Krkan if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. I've already seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that you look around the courtroom, and if you recognise him, please tell us where he is and what he's wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's wearing a lilac suit, violet suit, a white shirt, a tie. He's lost a little weight. His hair, well, it's slightly grey, but it's almost the same as it was. He's looking straight at me. Perhaps he remembers what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, could you tell us, please, where he is seated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's sitting straight over there, directly opposite. The first chair from the beginning of the table. There's the policeman, and then Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're looking at the area, is it the first table or the table against the wall that he's sitting at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last row next to the window, next to the glass, the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note a positive identification of Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also testified about Prcac. Do you believe you would be able to recognise him today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting at the first table. There's a thermos flask, a black one in front of him. He has a grey suit, a white shirt. He's got a moustache, and he's little greyer than he used to be, and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also note a positive identification of Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, could you please tell for the Court what physical effects, if any, you suffered as a result of your detention in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: You can't describe it. Quite simply, I'm quite lost now. I feel quite lost in my life now. Everything I had, everything that I wished for, for my life, the camp did to me that I seem -- I'm dead for everything. I have no wish to live. They've destroyed everything, all my property, everything that I had acquired. They destroyed my health. I have suffered terrible trauma. I suffer from insomnia. What more can there be? They've destroyed everything. And how can I carry on living a life like this because I'm not 70 years old yet. I can't just wait for death. I'm still a fairly young woman. I have children. I lost my husband, and he died a year ago because the camp affected him, too, and I have to take all this, to suffer it all. What caused it all was a war, our friends, our colleagues, our neighbours. The awful thing was that they were all my colleagues and that they did this to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, you talked about your husband. What physical --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What physical effects did your husband suffer as a result of his detention at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband was taken to the "white house" in Omarksa but he didn't arrive in the "white house." They did not beat him, but his kidneys suffered. The doctor said that both his kidneys had stopped functioning. He had to receive dialysis treatment. He had stomach pains from the nervousness. He never slept. He lost a lot of weight. He always said, "What have we come to? We have nothing. What are we going to do in the future? How can our children continue to live? I want to have my own house, my own place, and I can't go back to my own place." I can't bear to see how my town has been destroyed and all my property destroyed. Everything that I had has been destroyed, and to what avail? Why did it have to happen? They should have stayed there and realised that we would go back to our own property. I always want to go back where I came from, and I'll do that one day because that's where I spent my life. All this is just an excursion for me outside my place of residence. It's just a temporary excursion for me. That's how I feel. All this had its effect, and my husband succumbed a year ago. Psychologically, it killed him, and he went before his time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, did your husband have any kind of kidney problems before his detention in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any kidney problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have just spoken about your property. Did you ever receive any of your property back from the Prijedor opstina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everything's been destroyed. Everything's gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been paid anything for your property that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Hollis. I think that this is an opportune moment to take a break. I should like to ask the usher to draw the curtains and to escort the witness out of the courtroom to give the witness a little rest. So, Witness, you have a rest and we'll have a rest too. But please don't get up yet, Witness. Please remain seated for a moment. We're going to take a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the accused be seated. Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic, it seems that Mr. Fila is going to take the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I will be the first one to cross-examine, and I will be followed by Mr. Jovan Simic, and that will be that as far as the Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Witness AT, now you will be answering questions that will be put to you by the Defence counsel. As you probably understand, the Defence counsel are doing their job here. They defend the accused, and this is how the justice is administered. Mr. Fila, I hope that you will be able to take full account of the balance that needs to be stricken here, and if there is any doubt as regards any question, we can always ask the witness if she prefers to answer your question in private session. Mr. Fila, your witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, my name is Toma Fila, and together with Mr. Jovanvic, we represent the accused Krkan, that is, Mladjo Radic in this case as his Defence counsel. By way of introduction, let me ask you something regarding the period of time prior to your arrival in Omarska. (redacted), (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You see, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President. I do apologise. I realise that it is now too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. I took notes about questions that were asked in private and questions that were asked in public session. So please think twice before you proceed with your question, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. President. I was trying to be mindful of the speed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also apologise to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we already met over the telephone on one occasion, Mr. Fila. You once called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean I personally called you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Fila. And you were called from the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the way the gentleman introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the town where you lived prior to these events, did you ever notice that there were some people by the name of (redacted) (redacted) who behaved in an extremist way prior to the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know those men, but they did not behave in that way, the way you just described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just interested in knowing whether you knew them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I knew them. They were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? What period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meeting of the local assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like all other residents, I was obliged to attend certain meetings and I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this entire area is, of necessity, going to bring out information which can identify this witness. It's already happened on several occasions with the names of several individuals who can be linked to a particular town. Now he's talking about a named commander of police. I suggest that to protect this witness's privacy, that we go into closed -- or private session until he gets through these types of details which will identify this witness. We've already noted four or five areas we're going to ask for redaction because they're identifying details. We feel it would better serve this witness's privacy if we were to go into private session for these questions. The witness cannot honestly be expected to answer truthfully and keep out identifying details.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine with me going into private session. The only thing I have a problem with is the fact that it cannot be used later on. Those portions of the transcript cannot be adequately used later on. But of course we can go into private session. I didn't mention the name or the surname of the individual in question, perhaps only the nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have finally received the interpretation. Yes, you're right, Mr. Fila, there are certain elements which enable identification to an intelligent person. If the objective is to protect the identity of the witness, perhaps it would be better to go into private session; however, we must not forget the public character of the hearing. So, Mr. Fila, we perhaps can apply the same procedure as before. You can request a private session for certain elements, certain details that you're going to use later on, and then you can request to go back into public session and continue with the presentation of the case. It is a very precarious balance indeed, and Mr. Fila, if you do not act in this way, that balance will be endangered, and it can be to the disadvantage of the witness and to yourself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what is happening with the booth, but I'm not receiving any interpretation. I apologise. Yes, I can hear you now, but I didn't hear you a moment ago. I'm sorry, Mr. Fila. Could you please repeat your question because I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not a problem. The way I'm going to ask a questions will be such that it will not be possible to establish the town or identity of individuals; but, for example, the witness can also provide answers containing that piece of information. The problem is how to avoid the mention of the name of the town, and that, that is not my mistake, Your Honour. I hope you understand where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We will try to do our best. We are now in public session. If there are any reasons to go right away into private session, we will do that. However, I constantly have to sign these orders regarding redaction of transcript, and be mindful of the protective measures. Let us try and do our best to achieve both objectives. Mr. Fila, would you now continue with your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). If you understand me, just nod your head 'cause I don't want to provide any additional identification information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another person that attended the meeting, (redacted) (redacted), and did he -- what did he say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Fila, but if you tell the name of the police chief, that certainly identifies the town to most -- anybody who does any research. So I tend to at this point subscribe to the notion that you're just as well served if we have this private -- pre-Omarska period in private session. You can be assured that the Judges are here and hear it and will take into consideration whatever are the relevant points, but it's too risky, I think, for this private -- for this personal information, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with you. I said it's really according to your wishes. I don't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, it would be therefore preferable to go into private session, and then you can ask all the questions you wish to ask, including identifying questions. But please try to finish with the identification questions during this private session, and then we will go back into public session. Let us now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet, Mr. Fila. Yes, now we're in public session. Mr. Fila, if possible, would you please pause between question and answer, and ask only one question at the time, if it is possible. It is going to be easier for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is the following: What happened in that place that we referred to, and what did those individuals talk about, without, again, mentioning their names or functions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pressure was exerted on the commander. He was supposed to sign some loyalty papers and to hand over power into Serbian hands. He was also supposed to surrender weapons. So the commander approached the citizens, the residents, because it was the local assembly of the town in question. They were supposed to make decisions, but they were unable to render any decision because the majority opposed the idea of wearing the Serbian cockade or the so-called cockade. That was the origin of the conflict at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the individual that said he would kill every one who would be wearing that particular typical sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that time, we all lived together, Muslims and Serbs. All of a sudden there was the separation between Serbs and Muslims, and that's why he said, "Whoever wears a cockade and not this common sign accepted by all, he would be dismissed."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like us to go back into private session once again because I need to mention three or four names, and then after that we will be speaking about the relevant events. I think that this is actually working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, without mentioning the names, please answer me the following question: Were those people extremists? Did they pretend to be leaders of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you believe to be extreme? Those people were Muslims. I'm very offended by that word. It's not the kind of word that I would use in my vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether they pretended to be leaders and did that play actually into the hands of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not pretend to be anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they leaders at all of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is common knowledge that (redacted) (redacted) of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No names, Witness, no names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me not to mention the names, especially when you come up with the words that offend me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the individuals that we mentioned before,(redacted) did he have a group of armed young men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see armed formations of the SDA with camouflage uniforms in your town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who was able to buy camouflage uniforms would wear them, and it was difficult for me to control the situation in any way, to follow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the formations, to individuals wearing uniforms. I'm referring to formations as groupings of people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). It's your mistake, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, we're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to know whether the witness knew the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis. Yes, Mr. Fila, but you mentioned the name. Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't know where the person lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm sorry. I will now give -- I'm really sorry, Judge Riad. I will give the floor to Madam Hollis. She wanted to say something. Let us hear her.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I was going to object to the statement made by counsel. He used the name. It's disingenuous for him to say he doesn't know where the person is from. In our earlier session, he indicated the person's name before. He, I believe, needs to be more willing to go into private session or he needs to control himself more because we are repeatedly getting violations of the regular procedure you've asked us to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We are running the risk of going into, I mean, unwillingly into some violations, as you said. Is there a technical possibility that the people in the public gallery could just hear it five minutes or three minutes later? Because even if we redact, there might be one person in the gallery who would hear it and the redaction becomes useless. So if there is two minutes, even two minutes delay, that could save the situation. If it's possible with the public gallery here, the way they do it downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: My understanding is there is a 30-minute delay on television but it's immediate for the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's it. Can we have it also here, with two minutes only here? That's the technical question which I submit because that will make things easier. We can always be for public, even where there is doubt. Otherwise, we will have to go to private more than we need. Can we ask the technical people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that what we have here is something that we really should be mindful of. Mr. Fila, you're the one who brought up the issue. We decided that -- we made an appropriate ruling, but you have already used a name. You used a name that had already been used before. I will not use it now because it will be in the transcript. Mr. Fila, I really don't know how to do this. Perhaps we should have a short break for you to be able to review your questions. I think we can apply the same procedure was with the Prosecutor. You can ask all of your identifying questions in private session, and only after you have completed that part of your cross-examination, we will go back into public session with the general story, or we will keep going back and -- from private session and public session. But we're running the risk of having accidental mentions of protected names. What do you prefer, Mr. Fila? If you tell me that you prefer to do everything in private session, then I really don't understand the initial objection that you made to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, first of all, Mr. President, because I mentioned the individual on two occasions, and I forgot that I had already mentioned him. I should like to go into private session only once, for only one more name, and then that will be it. There will be no more identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Let us now go into private session for this question, but please wait a little, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a good suggestion. Madam Registrar, would you give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the number, may I please have five copies of that, and I always have to remind you that we need five copies. Three copies for the Judges, one copy for the Registry, and one copy for the senior legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, I know that full well, but it was not my intention to tender it into evidence. So why do you want five copies of something I did not wish to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's only for identification. Even if you're not going to tender into exhibit, we still need the number of that only for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are now faced with this situation. Mr. Fila does not want to tender this into evidence. Madam Hollis, would you like to have it marked or a number assigned? Because it is up to us to decide. That is to say, the parties can use the document. They are part of the preliminary documents in a way. So the statements given by the witness are, in a way, official, and we decided that the parties can use the document but need not have it admitted into evidence, so that they should be marked for identification. This would allow us to discuss the question of admission. But Mr. Fila does not wish to have the evidence admitted. So having said that, Madam Hollis, give us -- just a minute. Let's have a bit order in all this. Madam Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution's position would be that whenever a document is used in court it should be marked as an exhibit, even though it's only marked for identification, and at least one copy should be given to the registrar so that there exists with this case a copy of everything that was used in the courtroom, whether it's admitted or not. Otherwise, we have reference to a document that was shown to a witness and then there will be no copy of it anywhere in the record and we will have to reconstruct it if it becomes an issue later on. So the Prosecution's position would be that we would have to have at least one copy of it marked, and the registry would have that copy and there would be an annotation that it was just marked for identification but not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem, and I'm speaking in my own personal name. I consulted my colleagues, but I have a question myself, and that is that if in the last week of the Prosecution case we modify procedure, Madam Hollis, we're going to change the criteria. Lots of documents were used in that sense and did not receive -- were not marked -- did not receive a number. So what are we going to do now? Are we going to take all these documents up, to assign them a number? Why this document and not the others? So that is the question that I have for you. We are in the last week of the examination-in-chief, and we have used a lot of documents in this courtroom that were not marked because they were not tendered following the ruling we took. Now, if we are going to make an exception, I'm afraid of upsetting the balance and striking -- equilibrium, but I would like to hear your opinions, Madam Hollis, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that at least on one other occasion the Prosecution has raised this same issue with documents that were used but not marked. It is the Prosecution's position that any document that is used, whether it's offered into evidence or not, should be marked for identification and dealt with so that at the appellate level, dealing with Judges who have not sat here, if the source of the questions, that is, the document itself, becomes an issue then the documents are appended to the record. Your Honours, if you are not disposed to do that, then the Prosecution would ask that at least more identifying information be put into the record so that later if this document becomes an issue it will be easy to determine what document it is even if the document itself isn't somehow appended to the record. So that would be our first preference, but a suggestion if Your Honours choose not to have the document provided and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, I'm asking you the following: Are you requesting this for all the documents, the ones that have already been shown the witness and were not marked for identification, all the documents that we used in the course of the trial, statements that were placed before the witness, and you say that those documents should all be marked for identification, is that right, that they should all be marked now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: May I ask you a further question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you aware of other instances during the course of this trial when you have raised the question specifically asking for documents to be identified and they have not been? You just alluded to one, but are you aware of others in which you have raised the specific request and been denied by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe when the request was raised, the document was marked. That's my recollection. And I, today, cannot tell you if it happened more than once, but I do recall one specific occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When your request was granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I recall no occasion asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I recall none either. I just wanted to get that for the record. So I don't see -- well, it doesn't appear to me that were we to decide in your favour this time this would create any big problem in terms of past records, from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess the problem, Your Honour, that Judge Rodrigues is alluding to and may very well be a valid one is there may have been occasions when a witness was shown a statement and for some reason it was not asked to be marked. Therefore, we would not always have asked it. So there would be statements that aren't in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. But if you had not always asked, certainly from your point of view, you must not have thought it important enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Or we did not stand up and ask it. But certainly we did not take action at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You did not take action at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So my concern is really to keep this record intact so that at the appellate level if there are issues, it can be reviewed as to exactly what document is in question. That's my concern about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand your overall point of view, but as Judge Rodrigues pointed out, we are now fairly well along --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- in the case, and it strikes me that if you thought it very relevant for a document to be marked for identification up to this point, I would have expected that you would raise it, and you suggest that the only time you raised it it was granted, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct. Every time we raised it it has been granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. And when you didn't raise it, we can assume that that meant that you didn't think it was that important.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We certainly waived our right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You waived that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're now discussing technical matters, and we have a witness waiting here. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On July 4th of this year, Your Honours entered a ruling on the way in which previous out-of-court statements would be used, and a few days after that ruling, at the request of the Prosecution, the procedure that was established was that the statement would be put before the witness in fairness to the witness, and those documents were not marked, nor were they admissible. In fact, since that time, Your Honours have ruled certain statements inadmissible when counsel requested it. So we've had a procedure since early July, and it seems now there is a request for a different procedure. I submit it has to be one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something, Mr. President. If what my learned colleague Madam Hollis is saying is true, why would I be spending one hour and a half here to read portions of the statement? Because according to your ruling, we were supposed to read portions of the statement which were then entered into the transcript so as to avoid the whole statement to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber believes that in the present situation, there is a difference in respect of other documents that we used previously, including preliminary statements of witnesses; that is to say, the Defence is to have a copy, and the Prosecutor also had the document at their disposal. In order to maintain the equality of the situation and in order to avoid the need to have the document again, the Prosecutor needs to have a copy of the document; that is to say -- let me just ask the question first of all. Does the Prosecutor have a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is a document that I actually received from the Prosecutor. It was in the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We are not going to treat this document differently in any way. In case of an appeal, both parties will have the document. We have the transcript. Mr. Fila has read the relevant portion of the document for the record. If there should be a problem in the appellate proceedings regarding the identification of the document, the parties will be able to produce the document and to compare it with the transcript because the document is appropriately identified in the record. Madam Hollis, we take note of your suggestion, but maybe for the future, because we will be creating a very complex and difficult situation, we will have to go back and review all of the situation in which a similar issue was brought up, and, as you know, at this time of the proceedings, three days before the end of the Prosecution case, it will be very difficult. If a similar issue should arise in future, we might again take it up and discuss it. However, for the time being, since you both have the document and since we have the quotation from the document in the record, we believe that it is possible to use the document again and to identify it if necessary. As Mr. O'Sullivan pointed out, it was our decision, it was our ruling which was made after lengthy discussions, and we managed to find a good balance between two different positions, the position of the Defence and the Prosecution. So now we believe that if we are going to make an exception -- if there was to be an exception, it was, I thought initially, it was because the Defence had brought up the document that the Prosecutor didn't have. But since it seems that both parties have the document, we're not going to upset the balance that was established in our ruling three days before the end of the Prosecution case. So we're not going to mark the document for identification because we have other ways of identifying the document in the future if it should become necessary to do so. . However, I believe that we have learned something from this situation for the future. So regardless of whether the document is going to be admitted or tendered, for that matter, it should be given an identification number so that we can easily identify the document in future. So we thank you for that suggestion; however, the Chamber has decided not to mark this particular document for identification so that it would not be given any different treatment from all other documents that have been brought up during this case. Since there are ways of identifying the document for future use if it is necessary, we have decided not to have it marked for evidence. We are not going to speak about an identification number of this document any more, and let us try to finish this cross-examination, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I hope that I will be able to finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: May I just add one thing? I do appreciate, I think from our mutual experience, the usefulness of having documents marked for identification. I don't think it in any way interferes with the prior practice laid down in July the 4th which was addressed, as I understood it, solely to the procedure for admitting or not admitting statements. While I will certainly go along with the majority on this ruling, I would suggest that before the Defence begins its case, the Defence and Prosecution might attempt to come to some agreement as to how these things might be handled during the Defence's case in chief, you recognising the fact that we might do it in the Defence case and not in the Prosecution is actually, if anything, an advantage on your side, so you might be willing to at least discuss the matter with them for the future, for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Fila, please continue with your cross-examination. Let me remind you that we are in public session at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me just finish with this issue. In the system where I come from, it is the Judge who decides which document will be admitted. There is no need for tendering documents into evidence. If you believe that the proposal of Madam Hollis should be accepted, I have no problem with that. As I told you, my position stems from my legal background to a certain extent, but there is no need to discuss this issue any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, as regards Status Conferences, we can perhaps take up the issue once again, but let us finish with this debate, this discussion, because we have a witness here waiting who has come here to testify and not to listen to our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified, Witness AT, that one of your duties in Omarska was to wash dishes and do some similar chores in the kitchen. You also mentioned the issue of water, and you said that it smelled, that it stank. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that the water was not potable water, adequate for drinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not conduct any analysis, but according to the taste, I don't think it was potable water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you say if I showed you a document to the effect that the water was actually drinking water prior to that time and after that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the assistance of the usher, please, and have the witness be shown the document. The Prosecutor already has the document, but we have additional copies if you need them. No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar, I think that we now need a number for identification. Yes, Madam Registrar, what is going to be the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is D30/3A for the B/C/S, and D30/3B for English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you managed to read the document that is in front of you? It is in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't. I don't know why I should read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to hear your comment on what it says here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the document, but I can tell you without looking at the document what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you, Witness, is what you think of this document. If you don't have any comments, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the document because I'm not interested in knowing what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any detergent while washing dishes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the person by the name of Borka Vrhovec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose nickname was Nena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did perhaps Krkan bring you something from that person while you were detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the president of the women's association in Omarska. It is a group of women with which I socialised before the war. She learned that I was in the camp, and she brought me something, a small onion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any clothes brought to you at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just received a pair of knickers with that parcel on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from rooms B10 and B11, were there any other women's rooms during your stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were only two rooms with two separate groups of women that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband spent seven days in Omarska, if I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came on the 24th, and he left at the time the list of names of detainees was read out. He left in buses. I don't know the exact number, must have been ten buses or more, and they took them to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days after his arrival was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You can do your own calculation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come he had lost so much weight during those eight days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that just tells you how many problems he was faced with. My hair had gone completely white within the period of 23 days that I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has never said her husband was only in the camp for seven or eight days. Counsel is misstating the evidence. She said he came when she came, and he left when names were called out and buses went to Turnoplje. She did not say he was there seven days, eight days. She didn't give a number of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that he had lost so much weight during the time that he spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not only himself, but all other detainees who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to room B1. Do you know, by any chance, whether Zeljko Meakic slept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have the photograph, please? I should like to indicate on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the big conference room with the oval table in it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know? I was only once brought to that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Exhibit 377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, please ask your question. The witness has the photograph in front of herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see room number B1, Witness. Do you know whether Zeljko Meakic used this room for sleeping? Did he sleep there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was brought to that room only once, on one particular occasion, which I will never forget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question had to do with Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name was already -- it was also mentioned -- actually, you reminded me of the name that I couldn't remember a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to go into private session at this point, but let me first ask one other question before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AT, does the name of Marija Zepter tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marija Zepter, why would I know that person?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. That is what I wanted to know. Did you during the night and during the day, during the night when you were staying in rooms B10 and B11, were you able to leave the room on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I was called out, for example, by Mr. Krkan. That was the only occasion where I could leave the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you leave the room on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was able to leave the room only when I was called out. I had to have some kind of escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like know whether you were able to leave the room without any escort and without having been called out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, from time to time I had to leave because I had to go to the toilet, but I was afraid because they were all around. I was afraid of being hit by something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, I would look around to see if anyone was in the corridor, and then I would leave the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a guard in the corridor during the night while you were sleeping in this room at all times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were in the rooms. They would show up in the corridor only from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actually locked up in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. If we had been locked up, they wouldn't have been able to enter the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if they showed up only from time to time, were you able to walk freely around? Were you able to go into the corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would use the corridor on their own. They had to use the corridor to go down into the yard or to go downstairs or go back upstairs. So when I needed to go to the toilet, I had to go into the corridor to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. What I want to know is whether there was an individual, a person who would always be posted in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would be the purpose of him being posted there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps to guard you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to go into private session, please, because I have a number of questions relating to the issue which was already the subject of one of the questions that were asked by my learned colleague, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in open session. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, do you remember several years ago who you talked to from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I tend to forget people's names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I now reside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the 14th of September this year you talked to somebody from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I do apologise, but perhaps we could divide up the question. You asked whether "you remember giving a statement to the Prosecutor on the 14th of September." This should be two questions. First: "Did you give a statement?" Second: "Do you remember the date?" If not, she says "nay," "no," but she says no to two questions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement to the Prosecution in September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean "September"? That was several days ago, September. It's now October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twenty days ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty days ago, I was at the place where I reside now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 14th of September you talked to somebody from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always maintain contact with them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give a statement? How did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a telephone conversation, not a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you remember the date when you came and left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
