utterances.text: Witness U, before Dragoljub Prcac divided the women into two groups that day, what were the women in the restaurant told to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness U. Mr. Jovan Simic is on his feet. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution is drawing conclusions when he says that before they were divided into two groups. We don't know whether they were divided into two groups. He read out the list, and that was that. He read the list, didn't divide them into two groups, and that's what the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Saxon, perhaps you will arrive at a conclusion, but would you like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can lay some more foundation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Perhaps it's important, but we have an objection, so please take it a little further in order to arrive at your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness U, when Dragoljub Prcac read out the names of the women in your group, what did the women in your group do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We went outside and boarded the bus. As for the women who stayed, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that event occurred that morning, what were the women in the restaurant told to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: A guard came up and brought us a cleaning cloth and pails to wash the walls and to clean the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained in the Omarska camp, were you told who was a commander or warden before Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, you have something to say? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I have received an answer, so I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if the answer was something else, you would have made an objection. It was convenient that way. Very well. No problem. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The women who were not to be transferred on the 3rd of August, were their names called out that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the armed conflict in 1992, Witness U, were you familiar with a man named Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would you see Mr. Radic before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Approximately in front of the SUP, in front of the fast-food restaurant. In that part of town. That's where I would meet him often. But let me put something right at this point. I knew him, but I didn't know that that was his name before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn the identity of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: When I came to the camp. The same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the same thing"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Like for Mr. Prcac. I learnt about that in the camp, and I learnt about Mr. Radic as well. I knew him before, but I didn't know his name. I didn't know his name and surname, and it was in the camp that I learnt this from the women. I learnt his name from the women. I quote, I learnt it from their stories, that he was the leader of a shift in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. I also learnt that while in the camp. His nickname was Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness U, how long after you arrived at Omarska did you first see Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The first time I saw Mr. Radic was the same day but in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the same day that you arrived in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your detention at Omarska, how often did you see Mladjo Radic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, fairly frequently. Usually at night during his shifts in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what parts of the camp would you see Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjo Radic I could only see in our room or in front of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could ask for your assistance again. If you could take the exhibit that was marked as Prosecution 3/150 -- it's a diagram -- and place a copy back next to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take the pen again that's in front you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take up the pen that's in front of you, Witness U, and mark with the letters "MR" where you would see Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness U, what would Mladjo Radic do when he came to your sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjo Radic called out Jadranka Cigelj several times, and she would go out. And something that I wish to say, to add, is, if I may -- may I say something positive? I would like to say this in this courtroom. Every time he was in the shift, he would bring some food, some good quality food which they probably ate, and he would offer us some of that food to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness U, how did the food that Mladjo Radic brought to your room compare with the food that you and the other prisoners normally ate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It was a big difference. The food that Mr. Radic brought was pieces of meat, schnitzel. It was good quality food, whereas the food that we ate in the restaurant was a very poor quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Radic would call out a woman named Jadranka Cigelj from the room. Could you observe Jadranka Cigelj when she would return to your sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. She was very much afraid. Her face was all red. She used to sit down on the mattress on which she slept. But in my presence at least, she didn't say anything for me to be able to tell you what happened to her when she was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the hour is nearly 5.00. This would be a convenient time for me to pause in my questions, if it would be convenient for the Court. If not, I could go on for several more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that for you, for us, and for all of us, it would be a good idea to take a break. We're going to stop at this point and continue tomorrow, but please don't move yet. I'm going to ask the usher to lower the blinds for you to be able to leave the courtroom. We have a matter to regulate, and perhaps we could take advantage of these two or three minutes to see to the matter with respect to the organisation of our work this week. This merit has to be decided. As you know, we have a request from the Prosecution to admit the statement of the witness Tariq Malik. In this motion, the Prosecutor tells us that the Defence has no objection to the admission of that statement. Can the Defence confirm what the Prosecutor has told us? Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have agreed on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. So we're going to make our decision accordingly. I think it is important. On the 29th of September, 2000, the Prosecutor filed a motion so that the Chamber admit the statement of witness Tariq Malik. In his motion, the Prosecutor has underlined that this statement should be treated in the same manner as expert witnesses' statements like Clark, Brown, Klonowski, and Alonso. The Prosecutor indicates that it is for these reasons that he is basing his argument on the basis of Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure, recognising that the statement of Mr. Malik does not fully fit within the framework of that rule. The Prosecutor finally specifies that the Defence counsel of the accused have been contacted, and that they do not object to the admission of the said statement as has just been confirmed at this hearing. The Chamber takes note, takes good note -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. I'm afraid there must be a misunderstanding, Your Honour. The Defence agreed that without an investigator's examination, in accordance with Rule 94, we accept expert statements; and if we have an expert statement, I think we do not need an interpretation by the Prosecutor of that statement. All we agreed to was that there was no need for Mr. Malik to appear here in court because we agreed to accept the statements. I think it would be a dangerous precedent if an investigator's statement were to be tendered. So our agreement was not that. The agreement was that Mr. Malik need not testify about the expert report of findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have to go back to the beginning, then. It's a rather strange situation we're in. Ms. Hollis, what was the result of your final agreement? And I withdraw everything that I have said so far because I think there's a misunderstanding regarding this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This does appear to be a misunderstanding. It was our understanding after speaking with the Defence counsel that they would not object to the admission of this statement, that in fact, Mr. Malik would be called to testify but not about matters that were contained in this statement. So apparently there is a misunderstanding because we certainly would not have put in our pleading that the Defence had no objection to the admission of this statement if they had told us otherwise. So our understanding was they would not object to the admission of this statement, so apparently there certainly is a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I said clearly -- because I'm reading what I have in front of me, and the transcript is going to speak for itself -- I was saying that we were going to deal with a question regarding a Prosecution motion for the admission of the statement of witness Tariq Malik. I asked the Defence whether there was any objection. The Defence told me none. I was talking about the admission of the statement of witness Tariq Malik, and I'm repeating myself because I said it twice, and I'm going to say it a third time, Prosecution motion for the admission of the statement of witness Tariq Malik. I asked the Defence whether there was any objection, and the Defence told me there was none, no objection. To what? To the admission of the statement of witness Tariq Malik. That is why I was starting to dictate the decision. Where are we now, Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry if there is a misunderstanding, but there are five Defence teams here who spoke with Mr. Keegan regarding this matter. Mr. Keegan insisted that Mr. Malik should testify. We said no, it is not necessary, because we are handing over expert statement, and once they're admitted in accordance with Rule 94 bis, there is no need for Mr. Malik to interpret what the experts have said. It will be up to the Judges, finally. After that Mr. Keegan came again insisting that Mr. Malik should testify because the reason was that through Mr. Malik, we would tender these exhibits. I'm very sorry if there was a misunderstanding, but it was just not on my part, but that was the understanding that all Defence teams had of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, you have no objection to the admission of the expert reports, and you believe that it is not necessary for the investigator to come to testify or to tender his statement. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I understand now. Ms. Hollis, did you attend that meeting where this agreement was reached with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was Mr. Keegan who reported to me at the conclusion of the meeting what the results of the meeting were and his understanding of what agreements had been reached. And we would also, Your Honour, direct your attention to a portion of the transcript of the 28th of September where Mr. Keegan indicates that: "It might be worth discussing that the Prosecution does not intend to call any further witnesses today. We filed this morning with the registry a motion for admission of the statement of the investigator Tariq Malik for consideration in conjunction with the reports of the experts which were submitted pursuant to Rule 94 bis. "The purpose of that statement was for the investigator to explain the linkages between the forensic evidence which was examined by the different types of experts. The Defence has agreed to this procedure, and that is reflected within the motion." This was stated in open court with Defence counsel present. There's nothing in the transcript to indicate any objection to that or any indication of disagreement on the 28th of September, so certainly now we are surprised to hear there is disagreement. Be that as it may, of course, the Court has to deal with the current situation. We believe for the same reasons we stated on the 28th of September that the information provided by Mr. Malik is relevant to these proceedings. Where he does in his statement refer to expert reports, it is simply in showing his connection or explaining different numbers that were assigned to different bodies. We believe that it should be admitted. It would expedite his testimony. If the report is not admitted, we would request permission to allow him to testify about these matters because we believe they are relevant and would be of assistance to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis. Excuse me, but the investigator, Tariq Malik, is not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And in another portion of the motion that we filed -- Your Honour, could I have just a moment to look at the body of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the body of the motion, we further indicated in the motion that we had discussed this matter with the Defence. They did not object. Based on our understanding of that agreement, we went on to say that, therefore, even if Your Honours were to determine that this report did not fall within the parameters of the Rule regarding experts, that no rights of the accused would be violated. Now that we do have an objection by one of the Defence counsel, of course, that argument would no longer be a persuasive argument, at least as to that counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Ms. Hollis, this means that you are still upholding the motion as it stands, knowing that there is an objection by the Defence. So the Chamber has to rule. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber is going to decide but not today, tomorrow. For today, we will stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a question by Judge Wald. She would like to know whether the Defence would agree to the presence of this witness -- no. Please ask your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'd just like to know if the position of the Defence is that this particular person -- leave his statement aside -- could be called as a witness, or you would object to his being called as a witness, and if so, on what grounds? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we cannot interfere with the Prosecution's strategy. We feel that the experts have provided their reports. We agreed that they be admitted, but we feel that they do not need any interpretation, especially not by a person who is not an expert in the area, and to link them with the facts. We are there to do that, and, of course, Your Honours. If they do call him, there's no way we can interfere with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tomorrow we will meet again at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of October, 2000 at 9.30 a.m. 25
